research.topic: Meta's hosted model API (Meta Model API) and the Muse model family, as of 2026-10-29
research.summary: The old "Llama API" is gone. Meta's hosted developer API is now called the Meta Model API. Its docs are at dev.meta.ai/docs; the old domains llama.developer.meta.com and ai.developer.meta.com/docs both redirect there. The base URL is https://api.meta.ai/v1 and auth is `Authorization: Bearer $MODEL_API_KEY`. It speaks OpenAI Chat Completions, OpenAI Responses and Anthropic Messages, and Meta has no SDK of its own: you use `pip install openai` with base_url set. Hosted models are: muse-spark-1.3 (recommended), muse-spark-1.2, muse-spark-1.1, two cheap contributor-tier variants (`-contributor`), muse-wonder-1.0 (preview, expensive), muse-image-1.0, muse-voice-transcribe-1.0 and sam-3.1. Muse Spark Open (816B MoE) and Muse Glimmer (30B) are open-weight only and not on the Model API. No Llama 4 model is listed. For HeyNavi: Muse Spark takes base64 JPEGs (up to 50 per request) and returns structured JSON via `response_format` `json_schema`. It also has documented object grounding on a normalized 0-1000 grid, which gives you a box and left/right position directly. SAM 3.1 takes a noun phrase plus an image, returns boxes, masks and optional confidence for $0.0025 per image, and returns nothing when there is no match. Muse Voice Transcribe has realtime WebSocket and REST endpoints, costs $0.18/hour and supports Korean. No text-to-speech endpoint was found, so use on-device iOS TTS. The biggest risk is latency. Muse Spark always reasons (`minimal` is the lowest setting; `none` returns HTTP 400). Every public latency figure is for xhigh/max effort or of unclear origin, ranging from about 1.25 s to 44 s, so the <2 s per-frame target is unverified and must be measured on day one. The $150 hackathon credit appears only in secondary sources; Meta itself says only "free Model API credits", and how to claim them is not documented publicly.

findings.claim: The official hosted API is now called the "Meta Model API". The developer portal and docs are at https://dev.meta.ai and https://dev.meta.ai/docs. https://ai.developer.meta.com/docs/ returns 302 to https://dev.meta.ai/docs/. https://llama.developer.meta.com/ returns 302 to https://dev.meta.ai/. https://developer.meta.com/ai/products/meta-model-api/ returns 301 to https://dev.meta.ai/products/meta-model-api/. An LLM-friendly index is at https://dev.meta.ai/llms.txt.
findings.notes: Redirects observed directly with WebFetch on 2026-10-29. Meta's Connect recap (Sept 24, 2026) says the Model API is "now generally available globally". Earlier third-party coverage called it a public preview.

findings.claim: Base URL is https://api.meta.ai/v1. Auth header is `Authorization: Bearer $MODEL_API_KEY`, and keys start with `LLM_`. Keys are created in the API keys tab of the dashboard at dev.meta.ai. Rate limits are shared by every key on a team.
findings.notes: The OpenAI and Anthropic SDKs do not read MODEL_API_KEY on their own, so pass the key explicitly.

findings.claim: The API is OpenAI-compatible: Chat Completions (POST /v1/chat/completions) and Responses (POST /v1/responses). It also serves Anthropic Messages (/v1/messages). Meta ships no SDK of its own; the docs say to use the OpenAI SDK (`pip install openai`, `OpenAI(base_url="https://api.meta.ai/v1", api_key=os.environ["MODEL_API_KEY"])`) or the Anthropic SDK with base_url https://api.meta.ai. LiteLLM works with model `openai/muse-spark-1.3`. Python 3.14 compatibility of the openai package was not checked.

Do not use the old `llama-api-client` PyPI package. Its latest version is 0.6.0 (Dec 18, 2025), it points to llama.developer.meta.com docs, and Meta's SDK page does not mention it. Third-party reports say the Llama API public preview (api.llama.com) shut down on July 6, 2026.
findings.notes: The July 6, 2026 date comes only from secondary sources; I found no Meta notice. The redirect of the old domain is verified (M1).

findings.claim: Llama 4 Maverick and Scout are not on the Meta Model API. The models page lists only Muse Wonder, Muse Spark 1.1/1.2/1.3 (plus contributor variants), Muse Image, Muse Voice Transcribe and SAM 3.1. Meta's open-weight page covers only Muse Spark Open and Muse Glimmer. Secondary sources say the Llama 4 weights remain downloadable and that Groq deprecated Maverick (Mar 9, 2026) and Scout (Jul 17, 2026).
findings.notes: Definitive check: GET https://api.meta.ai/v1/models with your key returns the models enabled for your team.

findings.claim: Muse Spark (Meta, hosted only, proprietary). Model IDs: `muse-spark-1.3` (Standard, "recommended for new work", supports reasoning up to `max`), `muse-spark-1.3-contributor` (no `max`), `muse-spark-1.2` (previous version; the docs say to use it for audio input), `muse-spark-1.2-contributor` and `muse-spark-1.1` (original, Standard only). Input: text, image, video, audio, PDF. Output: text only. Context: 1,048,576 tokens. Max output tokens are not published. On muse-spark-1.3, audio input is "not fully supported".
findings.notes: Muse Spark 1.3 was released Sept 2, 2026 (propakistani, letsdatascience). OpenRouter also lists a dated alias, muse-spark-1.3-20260902; I did not confirm that ID works on Meta's own API. An Artificial Analysis page calls 1.3 "deprecated", which conflicts with Meta's docs; trust Meta's docs.

findings.claim: Muse Spark pricing per 1M tokens. Standard (1.1/1.2/1.3): input $1.25, cached input $0.15, output $4.25. Contributor (1.2/1.3 -contributor): input $0.10, cached $0.002, output $0.20. Contributor mode gives Meta permission to use your prompts and completions to train future models. Reasoning tokens are billed as output. There is no long-context premium. Web search grounding costs an extra $2.50 per 1,000 queries.

Rate limits are per team. muse-spark-1.3, 1.2, 1.1 and muse-wonder-1.0: 3,000 RPM and 4,000,000 TPM each. The -contributor models: 150 RPM and 3,000,000 TPM. sam-3.1: 3,000 RPM. muse-image-1.0: 150 RPM. muse-voice-transcribe-1.0: 256 concurrent streams and 16,000 streams per hour. A 429 should be retried with exponential backoff plus jitter, honoring Retry-After. Responses carry x-ratelimit-* headers (not on voice).
findings.notes: No tier or increase process is documented. Even the contributor limit of 150 RPM covers one request every 1-2 s.

findings.claim: Image input on Muse Spark. Chat Completions uses `{"type":"image_url","image_url":{"url":"data:image/jpeg;base64,..."}}`; Responses uses `{"type":"input_image","image_url":"<url or data URL>"}` or a file_id. Both base64 data URLs and http(s) URLs work. Limits: 50 MB inline, 1 GiB via the Files API. Formats: JPEG, PNG, GIF, WebP, x-icon. Up to 50 images per request; more returns HTTP 400. Only user-role messages are processed for images. Cost scales with resolution: a ~1280px image is about 1,300-1,500 tokens, and a short text-only request carries about 110 tokens of overhead. Exact counts come from POST /v1/responses/input_tokens. No max pixel size and no `detail` parameter are documented.

Object grounding ("perception grounding") is documented for Muse Spark. Coordinates use a normalized 0-1000 grid, origin top-left. Output shapes: point `{x,y}`, box `{"bbox":[{x_min,y_min,x_max,y_max}]}`, count `{points:[...],count}`. Objects not found are left out. Meta's tips: start box prompts with "You are an object grounding expert", keep the system prompt minimal, use structured output, and clamp values such as 1001.
findings.notes: Left/center/right can be read off bbox x-center: below 333 is left, above 667 is right. Accuracy figures are not published.

findings.claim: Structured output on Chat Completions: `response_format={"type":"json_schema","json_schema":{"name":...,"schema":{...},"strict":true}}`. `strict` defaults to false, and output is constrained to the schema either way. On Responses the parameter is `text.format`; each endpoint rejects the other's parameter. The Python OpenAI SDK's `client.beta.chat.completions.parse()` accepts a Pydantic model. Strict mode requires an object root, `additionalProperties:false` and every key listed in `required`; recursive schemas are not allowed.
findings.notes: The docs do not say whether structured output can be streamed.

findings.claim: Chat Completions parameters. Supported: stream (SSE), tools, tool_choice, max_completion_tokens (max_tokens is a deprecated alias), temperature (docs advise leaving it unset), top_p, reasoning_effort (minimal|low|medium|high|xhigh), prompt_cache_key. Not supported: logprobs, n>1, stop, frequency_penalty, presence_penalty, logit_bias, any `modalities`/audio output, web_search_options. Tool calling: tool_choice accepts only "auto"; parallel_tool_calls defaults to true; tool-call arguments stream incrementally. Use the `developer` role for instructions.

Reasoning cannot be turned off on Muse Spark or Muse Wonder. `reasoning_effort` (Chat) or `reasoning.effort` (Responses) accepts none/minimal/low/medium/high/xhigh/max, but `none` returns HTTP 400 on Muse models, and `minimal` is the shortest pass. Without the parameter, the model picks its own level. Reasoning tokens count toward max_completion_tokens and can truncate the visible answer. In streaming mode, expect a delay before the first visible chunk.

Muse Spark latency at low effort is not published. Artificial Analysis measures only xhigh/max with 10k-token inputs. For 1.3 at max: TTFT about 39 s, time to first answer token about 44 s, about 188-202 tok/s. For 1.3 at xhigh: time to first answer token about 25-29 s, about 235-295 tok/s. An Artificial Analysis comparison page lists TTFT 1.25 s for Muse Spark 1.1 (xhigh). OpenRouter shows P50 latency of about 3.69 s for muse-spark-1.3-contributor (variant and window unclear).
findings.notes: These figures conflict and none matches HeyNavi's setting: minimal effort, one small image, short JSON output. The <2 s target can only be confirmed by measuring it yourself.

findings.claim: Prompt caching is automatic: a stable prefix is cached with no flag needed. `prompt_cache_key` raises hit rates. On Responses, `prompt_cache_retention:"24h"` asks for longer retention (a hint, not a guarantee). Cache hits skip prefill and lower TTFT. Cached input on Muse Spark Standard costs $0.15/M.
findings.notes: The docs do not say whether images are cached. Put the fixed system/developer prompt first and the frame last.

findings.claim: Muse Wonder (Meta, hosted, proprietary, preview). ID: `muse-wonder-1.0`, Standard mode only. Input: text, image, video, audio, PDF. Output: text. Context: 1,048,576 tokens. Reasoning from minimal to max. Price per 1M tokens: $4.00 input, $0.20 cached, $20.00 output. Limits: 3,000 RPM and 4M TPM. Launched Oct 12, 2026. "Muse Wonder Full" is available only in Muse Code subscriptions, not on the Model API. Third-party figures put Wonder's TTFT around 19-32 s (Artificial Analysis-attributed) or 2.81 s P50 (Zenmux gateway).
findings.notes: Specs and pricing are verified from Meta docs. The latency figures are third-party and unverified.

findings.claim: SAM 3.1 (Meta, hosted). ID: `sam-3.1`, called through POST /v1/responses. Input: one user message with an `input_text` noun phrase (one concept per request, e.g. "chair") and an `input_image` (URL or base64 data URL), or an `input_video`. Output: special-token text in output_text, e.g. `<0f>0<|box;x1=..;y1=..;x2=..;y2=..;w=W;h=H|><|mask;...|>`, with boxes in pixel coordinates. output_text is empty when nothing matches. `metadata.include_confidence:"true"` (a string) adds a `c` score from 0 to 1. `metadata.mask_encoding:"one_bit"` makes payloads smaller. Streaming is recommended. Parser libraries: `meta_sam_parser` (pip) and `@meta-sam/parser` (npm). Price: $2.50 per 1,000 images, or $0.20 per 1,000 video frames with a 50-frame minimum. Limit: 3,000 RPM.
findings.notes: There is no documented option to skip masks, and no latency figures or max image size are published.

findings.claim: Muse Voice Transcribe (Meta, hosted). ID: `muse-voice-transcribe-1.0`. Realtime: WebSocket wss://api.meta.ai/v1/asr/realtime. The first JSON frame must arrive within 10 s and carries `authorization.accessToken:"Bearer <key>"` (the HTTP Authorization header is ignored), `audioEncoding` (`PCM_24KHZ`|`PCM_16KHZ`, s16le mono), `model`, `mode` (`PUSH_TO_TALK` default|`ENDPOINTING`|`DIARIZATION`), `partialMode` (`CUMULATIVE`|`DELTA`), `languageBias` (language names, e.g. ["English","Korean"]) and `keywords`. Events: speechStart, transcript {transcript, final}, speechEnd, speechComplete, audioProgress, error. End with `{"type":"endStream"}` and keep reading until close code 1000. Batch: POST /v1/asr/transcribe, multipart with a `request` JSON part and an `audio` part (mono 16-bit PCM WAV at 16 or 24 kHz, up to 10 min, 32 MB); can return JSON or SSE. Supports 25 languages with code-switching, including English and Korean. Price: $0.18 per hour, billed per whole second; streaming and batch cost the same.
findings.notes: No latency figures are published. The docs recommend PUSH_TO_TALK for voice commands and ENDPOINTING for voice agents.

findings.claim: The Meta Model API has no text-to-speech endpoint. The docs index has no TTS page, and Chat Completions rejects audio output (`modalities`/`audio` returns HTTP 400). Spoken output has to come from on-device TTS or another provider.

Muse Spark Open (Meta, open weights, not on the Model API). 816B-total / 42B-active sparse MoE with 256 experts. Input: text, image, audio, video. Output: text. Context: 1,048,576 tokens. License: Muse Model License; products must show "Built with Muse Spark Open". HF repo: meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B. Checkpoints: BF16 (about 1.65 TB) and NVFP4 (about 537 GB). Hosted by Baseten, Fireworks AI, Groq, Modal, Nebius, Together AI, OpenRouter and others. Third-party listings give the Fireworks ID as `accounts/fireworks/models/muse-spark-open`.
findings.notes: Meta specs are verified. The Fireworks model ID string comes from third-party catalogs only (unverified), and per-provider latency is unknown.

findings.claim: Muse Glimmer (Meta, open weights, Apache 2.0, self-host only according to Meta's docs). 30B dense model (about 2B vision encoder plus 28B decoder), distilled from Muse Spark. Input: text and image (video without audio). Output: text. Context: 128K by default per Meta docs. Released Aug 10, 2026. HF repos: meta-models/Muse-Glimmer-30B, -GGUF, -assistant. Runs on vLLM, SGLang, llama.cpp and Ollama; Meta says it fits a single GPU or a Mac Mini. Not on the Model API.
findings.notes: A 30B model is not practical on an iPhone. Nothing was found on hosted endpoint IDs or latency.

findings.claim: Other hosted model: `muse-image-1.0` (text+image in, image out; $0.01 per image; 150 RPM). HeyNavi does not need it.

Hackathon credits. Meta's Connect recap says only "free Model API credits". Secondary sources say each participant gets $150 in Meta Model API credits. The official event page (dev.meta.ai/events/global-hackathon) confirms the dates (submissions due Nov 4, 9:00 PM ET) and encourages using the Muse Spark series, Muse Image and SAM 3.1, but publishes no claim steps. /events/global-hackathon/rules returns 404. The help center has no credits article. Billing is postpaid: usage charges hit your payment method when the balance reaches a threshold, plus a monthly charge on the 1st. Baseten, Modal and Fireworks credits are not mentioned on any Meta page I found.
findings.notes: The $150 amount is unverified from a primary source. The claim process was not found publicly; it probably comes through the acceptance email, Discord or the dashboard.

findings.claim: Availability: per Meta's help center, the Model API "is available in most countries and territories where Meta AI is available and billing is supported". It points to a Geographic Use Policy but gives no country list.
findings.notes: Whether South Korea is supported, if the developer bills from there, is unconfirmed.

research.recommendation:
Backend client: from FastAPI, use the `openai` Python SDK with `AsyncOpenAI(base_url="https://api.meta.ai/v1", api_key=os.environ["MODEL_API_KEY"])` and Chat Completions. Pydantic models go to `client.beta.chat.completions.parse()` (or to `response_format` `json_schema` with `strict: true`). Use plain `httpx` for SAM 3.1 (Responses endpoint) and for the voice REST endpoint. Keep the key server-side only, and skip `llama-api-client`.

First thing to do (day 1): run `GET /v1/models` to confirm which IDs the team can use. Then time 20 calls each of muse-spark-1.3 at `reasoning_effort="minimal"` (one ~640-768px JPEG, short JSON schema, `max_completion_tokens` about 512), muse-spark-1.3-contributor, and sam-3.1. Every published latency figure is for high effort, so this measurement decides the design.

(a) Per-frame object search and position:
- First choice: sam-3.1 as the per-frame detector. Send the noun phrase from the goal (e.g. "chair") plus the frame, with `metadata.include_confidence:"true"` and `mask_encoding:"one_bit"`.
- An empty `output_text` means not found. A box gives you left/center/right directly from x-center against w, with no reasoning delay.
- Cost: $0.0025 per frame, so about 6,000 frames (around 2.5 hours of looping at 1 frame per 1.5 s) costs about $15.
- Confirm across 2-3 frames in a row with confidence above a threshold before speaking.
- Use muse-spark-1.3 (Standard, minimal effort) only when you need wording or a second check, e.g. "is it the user's chair, any obstacle nearby?". Ask for the documented grounding JSON: bbox on the 0-1000 grid, `found` boolean, `position` enum left/center/right, short description.
- Fallback 1: if SAM latency or the Korean-to-English noun mapping is a problem, run muse-spark-1.3 minimal alone with the grounding schema.
- Fallback 2: if Spark minimal is over 2 s, run requests back to back with one in flight at a time, never queued. Downscale frames to about 512px at JPEG q≈0.6, and put the fixed developer prompt first so automatic prompt caching applies.
- Scene description on request: muse-spark-1.3 at minimal or low effort, streamed, so the client can start TTS on the first sentence.

(b) OCR and sign reading: muse-spark-1.3, `reasoning_effort="low"`, one higher-resolution frame (about 1280px, roughly 1,500 tokens, about $0.002), streamed. Fall back to muse-spark-1.2 if 1.3 behaves badly.

(c) Voice-command intent parsing:
- First, a deterministic keyword/regex parser on the backend for the core commands in English and Korean: find X, stop, describe, read, faster/slower. This answers instantly at no cost.
- Fall back to muse-spark-1.3 minimal with a small strict `json_schema` (intent enum, target noun phrase normalized to English for SAM, language). Function tools would also work, but tool_choice only supports "auto", so JSON schema is the safer route.
- Contributor-mode models cost about 12x less, but Meta may train on the data. Use them only for synthetic or dev traffic, never for real users' camera frames or voice, and say so in the submission if you use them.

(d) Speech-to-text: muse-voice-transcribe-1.0 at $0.18/hour, which is negligible.
- Simplest path in 6 days: record a short mono 16 kHz 16-bit WAV clip on the phone (push-to-talk), upload it to FastAPI, and POST it to /v1/asr/transcribe with `languageBias` ["English","Korean"] and keywords set to common object names.
- Better path: stream PCM from the phone through the backend to wss://api.meta.ai/v1/asr/realtime in ENDPOINTING mode with `partialMode` CUMULATIVE. This needs raw PCM capture in Expo. As a further fallback, use on-device iOS speech recognition.

Text-to-speech: Meta has no TTS endpoint, so use on-device iOS TTS (e.g. expo-speech with ko-KR/en-US voices and rate control) and implement barge-in locally.

Avoid muse-wonder-1.0 for the realtime loop: it costs $4/$20 per 1M tokens and has high reported TTFT. Llama 4 is not on the API. Muse Spark Open and Muse Glimmer would need third-party hosting or self-hosting, so treat them only as emergency fallbacks if you have Fireworks, Baseten or Modal credits.

Budget: about $15 for SAM, $10-25 for Spark calls and under $1 for STT keeps development plus demo well under $150. Cap `max_completion_tokens`, since reasoning tokens are billed as output.
risks: Latency is unverified. Muse Spark always reasons and cannot be set to 'none'. Every published TTFT is at xhigh/max effort (25-44 s) or of unclear origin (1.25-3.7 s), so per-frame Muse Spark calls may exceed the 2 s budget even at 'minimal'.
SAM 3.1 has no published latency or maximum image size, and it returns masks along with boxes (there is no documented boxes-only option), so payload size and parse time need measuring.
SAM 3.1 takes one concept per request as a noun phrase. Korean goals ('의자 찾아줘') must be turned into an English noun phrase first, which adds an intent-parsing step to the search loop.
Reasoning tokens are billed as output and count toward max_completion_tokens. Uncapped requests can cost more than expected or have their visible JSON cut off.
Contributor-tier models are much cheaper, but Meta may use the prompts and images to train future models. That is a privacy problem for blind users' home camera frames and voice.

The $150 credit amount and how to claim it are not confirmed by a primary source. Billing is postpaid to a payment method, so the account may need a card on file, and credits might not cover every model (SAM, Voice, Contributor).

Muse Voice Transcribe realtime needs raw 16/24 kHz s16le PCM over a WebSocket with the key in the handshake. Streaming that from Expo on iPhone, without exposing the key, needs native PCM capture and a backend relay. The batch WAV path is simpler but slower.
The Meta Model API has no TTS, so spoken output and barge-in rely entirely on on-device iOS speech synthesis.
Model IDs change often (1.1 to 1.2 to 1.3 between July and September 2026). Hard-coded IDs could break; read them from config and check GET /v1/models.
Availability depends on country and billing support. If the developer's billing country is unsupported, access may be blocked.
open_questions: Which model IDs does GET https://api.meta.ai/v1/models return for the team's key? This confirms access to muse-spark-1.3, the -contributor variants, sam-3.1 and muse-voice-transcribe-1.0.

Actual p50/p95 latency of muse-spark-1.3 with reasoning_effort='minimal' on a single ~640-768px JPEG plus a short json_schema output, and of sam-3.1 on the same frame. Only a live benchmark from the developer's network can answer this.

How were the $150 hackathon credits delivered: acceptance email, Discord, coupon or auto-applied to the dashboard team? Do they cover SAM 3.1, Voice Transcribe and Contributor-mode usage, and is a payment method required?
Are Baseten, Modal or Fireworks credits actually part of this hackathon? No Meta page I found mentions them.
Does sam-3.1 handle Korean noun phrases, or only English? (Undocumented.)
How accurate is Muse Spark's 0-1000 bbox grounding on cluttered indoor scenes such as chairs, doors and cups? Accuracy is not published.
Is South Korea (or wherever the developer's billing address is) a supported country under the Meta Model API Geographic Use Policy?

Can the Expo app capture raw PCM for the realtime ASR WebSocket without a custom dev build, given that full Xcode and EAS are not installed? (Outside this topic, but it decides which STT path is realistic.)

verdicts.correction: I re-fetched all three redirects: ai.developer.meta.com/docs/ returns 302 to dev.meta.ai/docs/, llama.developer.meta.com returns 302 to dev.meta.ai/, and developer.meta.com/ai/products/meta-model-api/ returns 301 to dev.meta.ai/products/meta-model-api/. llms.txt exists. The Connect recap says the Model API is "now generally available globally".

The authentication page confirms the Bearer header, the MODEL_API_KEY variable, the LLM_ key prefix, the API keys tab, and that keys on the same team share rate limits. It also says explicitly to keep keys out of mobile and browser code and to proxy through your own server.

Endpoints, SDK guidance and base URLs are confirmed, and Meta's SDK page does say LiteLLM works with an `openai/` prefix. But LiteLLM's own page (the cited source) documents a native `meta/` provider: it shows `meta/muse-spark-1.1`, has a realtime ASR route at wss://api.meta.ai/v1/asr/realtime, and reads META_API_BASE. It never mentions `openai/muse-spark-1.3`. The open question on Python 3.14 is settled: openai 3.41.0 (Oct 28, 2026) requires Python >=3.10 and lists 3.14 in its classifiers.

Confirmed that llama-api-client 0.6.0 was released Dec 18, 2025, that it points to llama.developer.meta.com/docs, and that Meta's SDK page does not mention it. The July 6, 2026 shutdown date still comes only from secondary vendor blogs (Spheron, eCorpIT); I found no Meta notice. The advice not to use the package is sound.
The models page and the open-weight page list no Llama models. The Groq deprecation dates are secondary-only and do not affect the design.

The IDs, modalities, 1,048,576-token context, the 1.3 audio caveat ("use Muse Spark 1.2, or Muse Voice Transcribe") and "Recommended for new work" are confirmed verbatim. Meta's models page has no dated snapshot IDs or deprecation notices. Artificial Analysis does label 1.3 "deprecated" in favor of Muse Wonder, but that is AA's own label.
The pricing table matches exactly. reasoning.md says reasoning tokens are "billed at the same rate as visible output tokens". Contributor mode is not available for Muse Wonder.

All limits match. Two additions: background responses have a separate cap of 600 new submissions per minute per team, and a realtime voice stream rejected for exceeding a stream limit closes with code 1013 (file transcription returns 429).

Image formats, the 50 MB inline and 1 GiB Files API limits, 50 images per request, the user-role-only rule, the ~1,300-1,500 tokens for a ~1280px image, and the absence of a detail parameter and a max pixel size are all confirmed. One addition from the error-handling page: with store=true, large inline base64 media can return 413 even when inference succeeds.

The grid, origin, output shapes, omission of objects not found, and the tips ("object grounding expert", minimal system prompt, pairing with structured output, clamping 1001) are all on image-understanding.md. The cited perception-grounding cookbook does not contain them: it is a food-dot HTML demo. No accuracy figures or reasoning-effort guidance are published. Roboflow's independent object-detection eval scores Muse Spark 1.3 at about 58.6% mAP@50 at low effort.

The response_format shape, the strict default of false (with strict:false behaving like strict:true), the strict-mode rules and the ban on recursive schemas (HTTP 400) are confirmed. The structured-output page does not say each endpoint rejects the other's parameter; it says a parameter from the other endpoint "does not configure structured output, even when accepted for compatibility". The Chat Completions page does say text.format returns 400 there. In openai-python 3.41.0 the canonical helper is `client.chat.completions.parse()`, which moved out of beta in 1.92.0. `client.beta.chat` still returns the same Chat resource, so Meta's beta call still works, but use the non-beta path. Streaming of structured output is undocumented.

Confirmed, including that tool_choice accepts only "auto" (anything else returns 400), parallel_tool_calls defaults to true, arguments stream incrementally, and system is treated like developer. Also: top_p:0 returns 400, seed is deprecated, and search grounding is not available on Chat Completions. The non-streaming request has a server time limit (504, value unpublished), and streaming is exempt.

reasoning.md says `none` is "Not supported by Muse Wonder or Muse Spark: returns HTTP 400", and that when the parameter is omitted the model reasons at a model-determined level. The cap is on max_tokens/max_completion_tokens (Chat) or max_output_tokens (Responses, minimum 16) and covers reasoning plus visible output. Reasoning summaries exist only on Responses.

Independent low-effort figures do exist and they are much worse than the researcher's range suggests. In Roboflow's Vision Evals (updated Oct 26, 2026), Muse Spark 1.3 at LOW effort averages 25.79 s per object-detection sample, 14.53 s for identification, 20.06 s for counting and 26.68 s for OCR. At high effort it is 39-51 s. Minimal was not tested. Roboflow also reports Muse Spark Open at about 7.4 s per vision sample (provider not named). The Artificial Analysis max/xhigh figures are confirmed (1.3 max: TTFT 44.18 s, 188 tok/s, 10k-token input). The 1.25 s and 3.69 s figures remain unexplained. Per-frame Muse Spark under 2 s should be treated as very unlikely, not merely unverified.

Caching is automatic. prompt_cache_key is a stable per-app key, not per-user, and replaces the deprecated `user` field. prompt_cache_retention accepts "in_memory" or "24h" as a hint. No minimum prefix length or image-caching behavior is documented. cached_tokens is reported in usage.prompt_tokens_details (Chat) or usage.input_tokens_details (Responses).

Specs, the $4/$0.20/$20 pricing, 3,000 RPM and 4M TPM, and the Oct 12, 2026 launch are confirmed. Missed: Meta's models page says "Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full aren't currently available in South Korea, on Model API or in Muse Code." The latency figures are still third-party only.

Endpoint, request shape, one concept per request, the box/mask token format (pixel coordinates; x2/y2 inclusive; w/h give media size), include_confidence as the string "true", lossless/one_bit encoding, empty output_text on no match, streaming recommended, and $2.50 per 1,000 images / $0.20 per 1,000 video frames (50-frame minimum) are all confirmed. Corrections: the pip package is `meta-sam-parser` (import `meta_sam_parser`), version 0.1.0 from Oct 6, 2026, Python >=3.10 including 3.14. `@meta-sam/parser` 0.1.0 is ESM-only, needs Node ^20.17 or >=22.9, and React Native support is undocumented, so parse on the backend. Additions: SAM also takes box and point prompts, and video input (MP4/MOV with H.264, H.265 or MPEG-4, up to 15,000 frames, 16 tracked objects). Because it runs on /v1/responses, store defaults to true. No boxes-only mode, image size limit, language support or latency is documented.

The URL, the handshake auth (HTTP Authorization header ignored), the encodings, modes, partialMode (default CUMULATIVE), languageBias as language names, keywords, the batch endpoint and its limits, the 25 languages including Korean, and $0.18/hour are confirmed. There is also a `speaker` event. Mode guidance is misstated: the docs recommend ENDPOINTING for "voice agents and low-latency voice commands", and PUSH_TO_TALK only when the app controls turn boundaries (a mic button). Missed constraints: the server rejects streams that run more than about 5 s ahead or stay slower than real time (close code 1008). Live sources must keep sending PCM silence. PCM_24KHZ has no default and must be set. Close codes are 1000, 1008, 1011 and 1013. No ephemeral or client-side tokens exist.

llms.txt (about 170 pages) has no TTS or speech-synthesis page. Chat Completions documents `modalities` ("any value returns HTTP 400") and `audio` ("No audio output"), and the Connect recap announced no voice-output model.

Meta's page confirms 816B total / 42B active, the modalities, the 1,048,576-token context, the Muse Model License, the HF repo, BF16 (~1.65 TB) and NVFP4 (~537 GB), and the launch partners Baseten, Fireworks AI, Groq, Modal, Nebius and Together AI. The page does not state 256 experts or a "Built with Muse Spark Open" attribution rule; those are unverified from primary sources. The Fireworks ID is now verified from Fireworks itself: `accounts/fireworks/models/muse-spark-open`, serverless on US-only capacity, $1.25/$0.15/$4.25 per 1M tokens, text and image input. On Groq (`meta-models/muse-spark-open`) it is an Enterprise-only limited preview, so it is not a practical fallback.

Confirmed: 30B dense, Apache 2.0, text and image input, 128K default context, the Aug 10, 2026 HF blog date, repos -30B, -GGUF and -assistant, and the Mac Mini claim (Connect recap). The HF blog itself lists one 80 GB H100 as the practical BF16 minimum. Wrong: it is not self-host only. Meta's Glimmer page names Fireworks AI, OpenRouter and Together AI as launch partners. Fireworks lists `accounts/fireworks/models/muse-glimmer-30b`, but on-demand only (not serverless). Glimmer is also a reasoning model, with reasoning_strength low/medium/high/xhigh (default high) and no documented off switch, so it is not obviously low-latency either.
$0.01 per generated image and 150 RPM. The Geographic Use Policy restricts Muse Image in India.

The official event page does not mention API credits at all; the recap only says "free Model API credits". The $150 figure also appears in a Techpresso newsletter marked "Together with Meta" (sponsored copy), which is stronger than random blogs but still not first-party docs, and gives no claim process or expiry. The event page confirms the Indie track ("individual builders and students"), submissions due Nov 4 by 9:00 PM ET, and Indie judging on "creativity, technical ambition, and whether it works". Its recommended-models line lists Muse Spark, Muse Image and SAM 3.1 and does not list Voice Transcribe. Billing is usage-based with threshold charges and a charge on the 1st; the page does not explicitly require a card before the first call. No Baseten, Modal or Fireworks credits are mentioned anywhere first-party.

The help-center quote is confirmed. The Geographic Use Policy does publish a Restricted Territories list (Afghanistan, Belarus, China incl. HK/Macau, Cuba, Iran, North Korea, Russia, etc.), and South Korea is not on it. Its only model-specific restriction is Muse Image in India. Separately, the models page says Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full are unavailable in South Korea. No restriction on Muse Spark, SAM 3.1 or Voice in Korea is documented, but Section 2.1 says access is limited to jurisdictions Meta has enabled.

missed: Independent low-effort latency data exists and is bad. Roboflow's Vision Evals measure Muse Spark 1.3 at LOW effort averaging about 25.8 s per object-detection sample, 14.5 s for identification and 26.7 s for OCR (https://playground.roboflow.com/models/meta/muse-spark-1-3). Muse Spark cannot be in the 1-2 s per-frame loop, even as a fallback. Treat scene description and OCR as 10-30 s background tasks, give immediate spoken feedback ("Looking..."), and stream.

Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full are not available in South Korea (https://dev.meta.ai/docs/models.md). The user appears to be Korean and the app targets Korean. Muse Spark, SAM and Voice are not listed as restricted, but availability must be confirmed with GET /v1/models from the developer's own account and country.

On the Responses API, store defaults to true. SAM 3.1 runs only on /v1/responses, so every camera frame from a blind user's home would be stored server-side by default, with no published retention period. Large inline base64 with store=true can also return 413 even when inference succeeds. Send store:false on every SAM and Responses call (https://dev.meta.ai/docs/protocols/responses.md, https://dev.meta.ai/docs/error-handling.md).

Realtime ASR pacing rules: audio must arrive at about real time, never more than about 5 s ahead. Streams slower than real time are rejected with close code 1008, and a live source must keep sending PCM silence. No ephemeral or client tokens exist, and the docs say to keep keys out of mobile code. A realtime path therefore needs a continuous PCM relay from the phone through FastAPI, which raises the cost of the 'better path' a lot. The docs recommend ENDPOINTING (not PUSH_TO_TALK) for low-latency voice commands (https://dev.meta.ai/docs/speech-to-text.md).

SAM 3.1 accepts short MP4/MOV video (H.264) with built-in object tracking, at $0.20 per 1,000 frames and a 50-frame minimum ($0.01 per clip). This is an alternative to per-frame image calls when confirming across frames: send a 2-3 s clip and get tracked boxes for every frame. Latency is unmeasured (https://dev.meta.ai/docs/sam/segmenting.md).

Media that fails Meta's content policy returns HTTP 400 `content_policy_violation`. Non-streaming requests hit an unpublished server time limit (504, do not retry unchanged), and 503 carries Retry-After of 60 s on overload. The loop needs explicit handling for each so it never goes silent on a blind user (https://dev.meta.ai/docs/error-handling.md).

Library versions as of 2026-10-29: openai 3.41.0 (canonical `client.chat.completions.parse`), pydantic 2.14.2 with pydantic-core 2.50.2 (cp314 wheels), fastapi 0.162.0, and meta-sam-parser 0.1.0, all compatible with Python 3.14 (PyPI JSON). @meta-sam/parser 0.1.0 is ESM-only with Node engine constraints and undocumented React Native support, so parse SAM output on the backend.

The hosted fallbacks the researcher suggested are mostly impractical. Muse Spark Open on Groq is Enterprise-only limited preview. Muse Glimmer on Fireworks is on-demand only (no serverless) and is itself a reasoning model with no off switch. Only Muse Spark Open on Fireworks serverless (US-only, same price as Spark Standard) is readily usable, and Roboflow puts it at about 7.4 s per vision sample.

The Indie track is judged on 'creativity, technical ambition, and whether it works', and the event page lists Muse Spark, Muse Image and SAM 3.1 as the encouraged models. A reliable end-to-end demo built on SAM 3.1, with Muse Spark used visibly but off the hot path, fits the rubric better than a fragile per-frame VLM loop.
verification.revised_recommendation:
Keep the researcher's overall client choice: FastAPI with `AsyncOpenAI(base_url=\"https://api.meta.ai/v1\", api_key=MODEL_API_KEY)` for Muse Spark and raw httpx for SAM and voice, with the key only on the server. Change these parts:

(1) Day-1 check. Before writing any code, call GET /v1/models from the developer's account and country to confirm muse-spark-1.3, sam-3.1 and muse-voice-transcribe-1.0. Wonder is blocked in South Korea. Then benchmark sam-3.1 on a 640-768px JPEG with stream:true, store:false, include_confidence \"true\" and mask_encoding \"one_bit\". Also time muse-spark-1.3 at reasoning_effort \"minimal\" once, only to size the scene and OCR waits.

(2) Active Object Search. Make SAM 3.1 the only per-frame model. Use one request in flight with no queue, ~1-1.5 s cadence, store:false, and parse with meta-sam-parser on the backend. Position comes from box x-center divided by w. Confirm when 2 of 3 consecutive frames have confidence above a threshold, then speak. If single-frame calls are slow or flaky, try a 2-3 s H.264 clip to SAM's video mode ($0.01 minimum per clip) and use its tracking for confirmation. Take Muse Spark out of the loop entirely; even low effort is about 15-26 s per vision sample in Roboflow's benchmark. Use it only as an optional asynchronous verifier after SAM confirms, never gating the 'found' announcement.

(3) Goal parsing. A deterministic English and Korean keyword map handles the common objects: chair, door, cup, bottle, phone, keys, bag, table and so on, e.g. 의자 to chair. Muse Spark minimal with strict json_schema is a slow fallback for unknown nouns only, and the app speaks 'searching for X' immediately.

(4) Scene description and OCR. Use muse-spark-1.3 at minimal or low effort via streaming Chat Completions to avoid the 504 non-streaming limit. Set max_completion_tokens with headroom for reasoning, speak an immediate 'Looking, one moment', and start TTS on the first sentence. Handle content_policy_violation, 503 Retry-After and 504 with spoken fallbacks.

(5) STT. Use batch POST /v1/asr/transcribe with a push-to-talk WAV (mono 16-bit, 16 kHz) and languageBias [\"English\",\"Korean\"]. Skip the realtime WebSocket: it needs a continuous real-time PCM relay with silence padding and can close on slow ingress. On-device iOS speech recognition is the fallback.

(6) TTS. Use on-device expo-speech; Meta has no TTS. Implement barge-in locally.

(7) Privacy. Use Standard (not Contributor) models for real camera frames and voice, and send store:false on every Responses call, including all SAM calls.

(8) Fallbacks. Muse Spark Open on Fireworks serverless (`accounts/fireworks/models/muse-spark-open`, US-only) is the only readily usable third-party fallback, and it is not fast. Do not plan around Groq (enterprise-only) or Glimmer (no serverless; it is also a reasoning model).

(9) Budget. The researcher's estimate stands: SAM at $0.0025 per frame dominates, and the total stays well under $150. Do not rely on the $150 until the dashboard shows it applied, and expect usage-based threshold billing to your payment method.

research.topic: SAM 3 / SAM 3.1 for real-time text-prompted object finding (HeyNavi Active Object Search)
research.summary: SAM 3 came out on 2025-11-19. It does promptable concept segmentation: you give it a short noun phrase such as "chair", image exemplars, or points/boxes/masks, and it returns a box, mask and score for every matching instance. SAM 3.1 (2026-03-27) adds Object Multiplex, a shared memory for tracking many objects at once, and its published speedups are for video tracking only. Meta published nothing on single-image speed for 3.1. The most useful finding for HeyNavi is that Meta already hosts SAM 3.1 on the Meta Model API as model `sam-3.1`, on the same OpenAI-compatible `POST https://api.meta.ai/v1/responses` endpoint and bearer key as the Muse models. It accepts a base64 data-URL image and costs $2.50 per 1,000 images, so the $150 hackathon credit buys about 60,000 frames. The rate limit is 3,000 RPM per team, and there is no GPU to manage. Its output is not JSON but a special-token text format (`<0f>0<|box;x1=..;y1=..;x2=..;y2=..;w=..;h=..;c=..|><|mask;...|>`), and zero matches come back as an empty output_text. Meta publishes a zero-dependency Python parser (`meta-sam-parser`) for it. Meta publishes no latency figure for the hosted endpoint, so the 1.5 s budget is plausible but has to be measured on day 1. The published model-side numbers are 30 ms per image (100+ objects, H200, from the paper) and 251.4 ms on one L4 (Roboflow, single text prompt). Self-hosting is possible through transformers `Sam3Model`/`Sam3Processor`, but only for SAM 3 (`facebook/sam3`, gated). SAM 3.1 checkpoints have no transformers integration, and the official repo needs a CUDA 12.6+ GPU. I found no published Apple Silicon timings, and MPS support is still in open PRs, so the Mac is not a viable runtime. Muse Spark 1.3 has documented visual grounding (boxes/points on a 0-1000 normalized grid) on the same API, which makes it a zero-setup fallback. Its weak spot is presence: a VLM may report or box an object that isn't there. That is why confirmation across frames matters.

findings.claim: SAM 3 was announced 2025-11-19. It is a unified model that detects, segments and tracks objects in images and video from concept prompts: short noun phrases (e.g. 'yellow school bus'), image exemplars, or both, plus SAM-style points, boxes and masks. It returns masks and unique IDs for ALL matching instances. Architecture: a DETR-based image detector and a SAM2-style memory tracker that share one vision encoder, about 848M parameters (the HF card shows 0.9B, F32). A presence head decouples recognition from localization: each query's final score is its own score multiplied by a global presence score.
findings.notes: transformers exposes presence_logits; per the docs, final_scores = pred_logits.sigmoid() * presence_logits.sigmoid().

findings.claim: SAM 3.1 ('Object Multiplex') was released 2026-03-27. It introduces a shared-memory approach for joint multi-object video tracking: objects are grouped into buckets (16 per bucket in the public checkpoint) and processed in one pass. Speed claims are all for video: about 7x faster inference at 128 objects on a single H100 (HF card), and 16 to 32 fps on one H100 for videos with a medium number of objects (Meta blog). VOS improved on 6 of 7 benchmarks. Meta published no single-image speedup for 3.1.
findings.notes: LearnOpenCV (secondary) says 3.1 also ships a newly trained detector and that some image metrics shift (e.g. LVVIS mAP 36.3 to 34.3). Treat the 3.1 single-image accuracy and latency as unknown.

findings.claim: Official repo: github.com/facebookresearch/sam3. HF checkpoints: facebook/sam3 and facebook/sam3.1. Both are gated: you must accept the conditions on HF and authenticate with an HF token. License: 'SAM License' (dated Nov 19, 2025). It is a royalty-free limited license that does not restrict use to non-commercial purposes, requires passing the agreement on with redistribution, and bars military/warfare, ITAR, nuclear and espionage uses. Repo requirements: Python 3.12+, PyTorch 2.7+, a CUDA-compatible GPU with CUDA 12.6+. Image API: build_sam3_image_model() + Sam3Processor(model).set_image(img), then set_text_prompt(state, prompt), returning masks/boxes/scores.
findings.notes: I could not find how long gated-access approval takes. Request access to facebook/sam3 immediately if self-hosting stays on the table.

findings.claim: Published latency: 'On an H200 GPU, SAM 3 runs in 30 ms for a single image with 100+ detected objects' (paper). Roboflow measured 251.4 ms mean for sam3 on 1x NVIDIA L4 (batch 1, after warmup, single text prompt). Video latency scales with object count, near real-time for about 5 concurrent objects (SAM 3). I found no official VRAM requirement or T4/A100 per-image number. Third-party reports: about 8 GB GPU memory on A100 (arXiv 2512.11884, per search snippet); about 4 GB at model load on RTX 4090; CUDA OOM on a 24 GB A10G with extremely dense small-object scenes.
findings.notes: The H200 and L4 numbers are verified from primary pages. The VRAM figures are third-party, and I did not open the arXiv PDF myself. Inferred: an L4 or A10G (24 GB) is enough for single-concept household scenes.

findings.claim: Hugging Face transformers supports SAM 3 (not 3.1) via Sam3Model and Sam3Processor (plus Sam3VideoModel, Sam3TrackerModel and Sam3TrackerVideoModel). It shipped in transformers v5.0.0+, and a v4.57.3 side branch also existed. Minimal code: model=Sam3Model.from_pretrained('facebook/sam3', device_map='auto'); processor=Sam3Processor.from_pretrained('facebook/sam3'); inputs=processor(images=image, text='chair', return_tensors='pt').to(model.device); with torch.no_grad(): outputs=model(**inputs); results=processor.post_process_instance_segmentation(outputs, threshold=0.5, mask_threshold=0.5, target_sizes=inputs.get('original_sizes').tolist())[0]. The results dict has 'masks', 'boxes' (xyxy, absolute pixels) and 'scores'. The model is meant for 1008 px input. A custom size (e.g. 560) runs faster but the docs warn it may degrade accuracy. Text embeddings can be precomputed with model.get_text_features() and reused across frames. facebook/sam3.1 has 'no Hugging Face Transformers integration'.
findings.notes: Precomputing the text embedding once per search goal ('chair') is useful for the HeyNavi loop if self-hosted.

findings.claim: I found no published per-image timing for SAM 3 on Apple Silicon (MPS, MLX or CPU). The official repo hard-depends on Triton (CUDA-only). MPS/CPU support PRs (#173, #400, #627) are open and unmerged; #173's author ran playground examples on an M2 Max without timings and hit OOM on batch inference. An HF discussion reports the transformers implementation works on Apple Silicon (video needed a pin_memory patch). MLX ports exist (github.com/Deekshith-Dade/mlx_sam3 / mlx-community/sam3-image, about 3.5 GB weights, Python 3.13+; mlx-community/sam3-8bit, 1.04 GB) but publish no latency. For comparison, SAM 2.1 Tiny with point prompts on an M1 via MPS took about 1.6 s per segmentation (blog).
findings.notes: Inferred, not measured: an 848M model at 1008 px on an M-series laptop via PyTorch MPS will probably miss a 1.5 s budget, given the SAM 2.1 Tiny datapoint. Use the Mac only for offline experiments. Python 3.14.7 on this machine may also lag torch wheel support; use a 3.12 venv for any local torch work (inferred).

findings.claim: Meta hosts SAM 3.1 on the Meta Model API as model ID `sam-3.1` (self-serve with login; web playground). Endpoint: POST https://api.meta.ai/v1/responses (OpenAI-SDK compatible, same Bearer key as the Muse models). Request: one user message whose content has an `input_text` part (a short noun phrase, one concept per request) and an `input_image` part whose `image_url` is a public URL or a base64 data URL (`data:image/png;base64,...`); video goes in `input_video` (video_url or file_id from POST /v1/files). `stream: true` is recommended for video, and non-streaming also works. Optional metadata: include_confidence:'true' (string) adds `c` (0-1) per box/mask, and mask_encoding:'one_bit' gives smaller masks (default 'lossless'). There is no threshold parameter and no boxes-only option, and the response returns every matching instance. Output is special-token text in output_text, e.g. `<0f>0<|box;x1=353;y1=382;x2=453;y2=427;w=537;h=561|><|mask;x=0;y=0;data=...|>`, with boxes in source pixels. Zero matches give an empty output_text with no delta events. Parser: `pip install meta-sam-parser` (Python >=3.10, zero deps; confidence needs >=0.0.6) or npm `@meta-sam/parser`. Box/point prompts use the same token grammar in input_text (up to 16 prompted objects).
findings.notes: The docs say a full Python request-plus-parse example is not on the client-libraries page, which shows only TypeScript. The Python parse entry points mirror TS (decode_mask_to_raster etc.), but I did not verify the exact Python parse function name for image streams. Image size limits and file-size limits for sam-3.1 are not documented.

findings.claim: Meta Model API pricing for sam-3.1: $2.50 per 1,000 images, and $0.20 per 1,000 video frames with a 50-frame minimum per video request. Rate limit: 3,000 RPM per team, shared across keys, no TPM limit. For context: muse-spark-1.3 costs $1.25/$4.25 per 1M input/output tokens at 3,000 RPM, and muse-voice-transcribe-1.0 costs $0.18 per audio hour.
findings.notes: Derived: at 1 frame/s, 1 hour of active search is 3,600 images, about $9. $150 covers about 60,000 frames, if hackathon credits apply to sam-3.1, which I did not verify.

findings.claim: SAM 3.1's availability on the Meta Model API was announced by @AIatMeta around 2026-09-18. I decoded that date from the X post ID that the Digg aggregator links; it is not stated on Meta's docs.
findings.notes: The date comes from the Twitter snowflake timestamp of status 2100994870282486044.

findings.claim: Meta publishes no latency figure for the hosted sam-3.1 endpoint. Its product page says only that inference is 'built specifically for its DETR architecture' and promises production throughput. LearnOpenCV states that hosted latency was not measured.
findings.notes: I searched dev.meta.ai docs and the web for ms/latency figures and found none. This must be measured.

findings.claim: Muse Spark (model ID muse-spark-1.3 in examples) supports documented visual grounding on the same API. It returns points ({x,y}), boxes ({bbox:[x_min,y_min,x_max,y_max]}) or counts on a normalized 0-1000 grid relative to the image sent. Values may slightly exceed the range, so clamp them. The docs say a prompt beginning 'You are an object grounding expert' measurably improves recall, and recommend pairing grounding with structured output. Images can be sent as URL, base64 data URL or file_id; up to 50 images per request; 50 MB per inline image. Meta's media-segmentation guide recommends using Muse Spark to decide what to segment and SAM 3.1 to localize it.
findings.notes: The failure modes are partly inferred. Expected issues: claiming or boxing an object that is absent (presence hallucination), coarse or loose boxes (Willison calls the 'pixel-level precision' claim overstated), frame-to-frame inconsistency, and higher, more variable latency than SAM. Evidence that VLMs are weaker at exhaustive concept detection: the SAM 3 README reports SA-Co/Gold cgF1 55.7 for SAM 3 vs 14.4 for Gemini 2.5.

findings.claim: Roboflow hosts SAM 3 on its Serverless API: POST https://serverless.roboflow.com/sam3/concept_segment (Bearer auth). The body takes {image:{type:'base64'|'url', value}, prompts:[{type:'text', text:'chair'}] (max 16), output_prob_thresh:0.5, format:'polygon'|'rle'}. The response has prompt_results[].predictions[] with confidence and masks (polygons), plus time. Measured latency: 251.4 ms on 1x L4. SAM 3.1 is not mentioned. The video tracker requires local GPU execution.
findings.notes: I could not find the per-call price or credit cost; the Roboflow credits and pricing pages do not list SAM 3 rates. Boxes are not explicitly in the response, so they would have to be derived from the polygons (inferred).

findings.claim: fal.ai hosts SAM 3 (not 3.1) as endpoint `fal-ai/sam-3/image` at $0.005 per request. Inputs: image_url plus a text prompt (points/boxes/masks also accepted), max_masks 1-32, include_scores, sync_mode. Masks come back as image files; boxes and scores are optional metadata. Latency is not stated. WaveSpeedAI also lists SAM3 Image from $0.005 per run.
findings.notes: The exact box-output parameter name is not shown on the page.

findings.claim: Replicate has only community SAM 3 models, no official one. mattsays/sam3-image runs on an L40S at about $0.0016/run, 'usually within 2 seconds' per the page (a search snapshot said about $0.00098 and within 1 s). yodagg/sam3-image-seg runs on a T4, within about 8 s. lucataco/sam3-video also exists. The input/output schema was not visible.
findings.notes: Community models may cold-boot (inferred), which makes them a poor fit for a 1.5 s loop.

findings.claim: Modal has no official SAM 3 example: the modal-examples sam/ folder contains only the SAM 2 segment_anything.py example. A community repo (TheFloatingString/sam3-on-modal) deploys the facebookresearch sam3 package on an L40S by default, with POST /infer_image {image_base64, prompt} returning {masks, boxes, scores} and the HF token stored as a Modal secret. Modal prices per second: T4 $0.000164, L4 $0.000222 (about $0.80/h), A10 $0.000306, L40S $0.000542 (about $1.95/h), A100-80GB $0.000694, H100 $0.001097. The Starter plan includes $30/month free credit. Warm-pool controls: min_containers, buffer_containers, and scaledown_window (default 60 s, range 2 s to 20 min). The pool can be changed at runtime without redeploying via f.autoscaler.update(min_containers=1) (for a Cls: obj.method.autoscaler.update(...)), including from a scheduled function. Containers boot in about 1 s, but warm-up (weight loading in @modal.enter) can take seconds to minutes. Weights should be baked into the image or a Volume. GPU memory snapshots are alpha and don't speed up weight loading.
findings.notes: Whether hackathon-provided Modal credits exist is unverified. Region selection costs a 1.15-1.75x multiplier and non-preemptible execution 3x.

findings.claim: Hugging Face: no Inference Provider currently serves facebook/sam3 (per the model page). A Dedicated Inference Endpoint with a custom handler.py is possible; community examples exist (peterproofpath/sam3, phongphamthe/inference-endpoint-poc). AWS hourly prices: T4 $0.50, L4 $0.80, A10G $1.00, L40S $1.80, A100 $2.50. Billing is per minute and includes initialization time. Paused endpoints don't count against quota.
findings.notes: Cold-start time for a scaled-to-zero endpoint is not documented.

findings.claim: Baseten's model library lists no SAM / Segment Anything model, and Fireworks' model catalog search shows no SAM model. Neither offers a turnkey SAM 3/3.1 endpoint, so either would need a custom deployment (e.g. a Baseten Truss).
findings.notes: The Fireworks catalog page only rendered 9 of 329 models, so absence is likely but not certain.

findings.claim: Lighter community alternatives exist. EfficientSAM3 and SAM3-LiteText (github.com/SimonZeng7108/efficientsam3) distill SAM 3 into TinyViT/MobileCLIP students. Ultralytics 8.4.148 release notes mention SAM 3.1 image-predictor support but no Object Multiplex video tracking yet.
findings.notes: No verified latency numbers. Not recommended with 6 days left.

research.recommendation:
PRIMARY (verified to exist; latency not verified): use Meta's hosted `sam-3.1` through the existing FastAPI backend, with no GPU to provision.
(1) The iPhone captures a frame, resizes it on-device to 640-1024 px on the long side, encodes it as JPEG q≈0.7, and POSTs it to FastAPI.
(2) FastAPI forwards it to POST https://api.meta.ai/v1/responses with model 'sam-3.1', an input_text noun phrase ('chair'), input_image as a base64 data URL, metadata {include_confidence:'true', mask_encoding:'one_bit'} and stream:false. It reuses one keep-alive httpx/OpenAI client.
(3) Parse with `meta-sam-parser`, keep only boxes with c, and ignore masks. An empty output_text means 'not seen in this frame'.
(4) Turn the user's utterance into one English noun phrase before calling SAM: 'find my chair' / '내 의자 찾아줘' → 'chair'. Use a regex for common objects and a cheap muse-spark call otherwise. That SAM's text prompts must be English is inferred, not verified.
(5) Confirm across frames: announce only after, e.g., 2 of the last 3 frames return the concept with c ≥ ~0.5 (tune this threshold). Direction comes from the box centre: x/w < 0.33 'left', > 0.67 'right', else 'ahead'. Box area / frame area gives a rough 'close/far'.
(6) Cost is $2.50 per 1,000 frames (about $9 per hour at 1 fps). Pause the loop when the app is backgrounded or the goal is satisfied.
Do this on day 1: get an API key, send 20 real 768 px frames, and log p50/p95 round-trip from FastAPI and from the phone. Meta publishes no latency, so the <1.5 s target is INFERRED from the 30 ms H200 and 251 ms L4 model-side numbers plus network overhead.

FALLBACK A (zero extra setup, verified docs): Muse Spark 1.3 grounding on the same key. Prompt 'You are an object grounding expert… return JSON {present: bool, bbox: [x_min,y_min,x_max,y_max] on a 0-1000 grid}' with structured output, then scale by the image size and clamp. This works for 'find my chair', but VLMs can claim objects that are not there, so require multi-frame agreement and phrase results cautiously ('I think I see…'). You can also use Spark as a verifier on the frame where SAM first fires.

FALLBACK B (minutes of setup): Roboflow Serverless `sam3/concept_segment` (251 ms published on an L4; pricing unverified), or fal.ai `fal-ai/sam-3/image` ($0.005/request; latency unknown). Keep the backend's SAM client behind an interface with providers meta_sam31 | muse_grounding | roboflow, so you can switch providers with an env var.

FALLBACK C (most effort, about half a day): self-host SAM 3 (not 3.1) on Modal with transformers Sam3Model + facebook/sam3. Request HF gated access today. Use an L4 or A10 (inferred sufficient; the L4 is $0.80/h), bake the weights into the image or a Volume, load them in @modal.enter, precompute the text embedding per goal, and expose a FastAPI endpoint taking {image_base64, prompt}. Deploy with min_containers=0 and scaledown_window of about 600-1200 s. Before a test or demo session, run a script that calls `obj.method.autoscaler.update(min_containers=1)` and sends one warm-up request. Afterwards, set min_containers back to 0, or use a modal.Cron pair around the demo slot. Three hours of warm L4 is about $2.40, inside the $30 Starter credit.

Do NOT plan on running SAM 3 on the M-series Mac. There is no verified usable speed, MPS support sits in unmerged PRs, and the official repo needs Triton/CUDA. Muse Spark Open/Glimmer are self-host only and irrelevant here.

Verified from docs: S1-S5, S7, S8, S11-S16. Inferred: end-to-end latency, the VRAM sufficiency of an L4, English-only prompts, VLM failure modes, and the warm-up cost estimates.
risks: Hosted sam-3.1 latency is undocumented. The phone-to-FastAPI-to-Meta round trip, plus base64 upload of a 768-1024 px JPEG, could exceed 1.5 s, especially on mobile networks or if the FastAPI server is on the Mac behind a tunnel.
No image size or file-size limit is documented for sam-3.1. Oversized frames could be rejected or slow, so downscale on-device.
The sam-3.1 response always includes a mask per object (no boxes-only mode), which inflates payload and parse time. Use mask_encoding 'one_bit' and discard masks.
There is no server-side confidence threshold. False positives must be filtered client-side using `c` (requires include_confidence='true' and meta-sam-parser >=0.0.6) and multi-frame confirmation.

Meta's docs say 'commands, questions, lists, negation, and spatial phrasing' are unreliable as prompts. Raw utterances like 'find my chair' or Korean text must be normalized to a single English noun phrase first (English-only is inferred).
Hackathon credits may not cover sam-3.1, or may be limited to certain models (unverified). The 3,000 RPM limit is per team and shared with any other Meta API calls.

VLM-only grounding (Muse Spark) can hallucinate presence or return loose boxes. For a blind user, a false 'found it' is worse than a slow answer, so phrase results cautiously and confirm across frames.
Self-hosting needs gated HF approval for facebook/sam3 with unknown turnaround. SAM 3.1 weights have no transformers integration, and the official repo needs CUDA 12.6+ and Triton.
Cold starts on Modal or HF endpoints (loading about 3.5 GB of weights) can take tens of seconds to minutes. Warm the container before demos, or the first query will blow the latency budget.
Community-hosted SAM 3 models on Replicate are unofficial and may cold-boot (e.g. a T4 version 'within 8 seconds'), so they are unsuitable for the live loop.
Fireworks and Baseten have no turnkey SAM; time spent there would be custom deployment work.
The SAM License bars military/ITAR use and requires passing the license on with redistribution. Fine for HeyNavi, but note it in the submission if weights are redistributed.

What are sam-3.1's maximum image dimensions and payload size, and does it downscale internally (the SAM 3 transformers default is 1008 px)?
Where will the FastAPI backend run during the demo (the Mac via a tunnel, or a cloud host)? This dominates network latency.
